examples.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
examples.worked_solution:
First,  notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $A=PDP^{-1},$ we can compute $A^k$ by using the formula 

$$
A^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{100} & =P{D}^{100}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{100}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{100} & 0 \\ 0 & {0}^{100}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $S$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
S={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & -12 \\ 10 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
